\begin{abstract}
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) raises the single-sample accuracy of language models, but
whether it also shrinks the set of problems a model can solve at all is disputed: some studies find base models
overtaking RLVR-trained ones at large $k$, others report expansion under longer training, and others trace the
decline to how Pass@$k$ is measured. The evidence on all sides is automatic (Pass@$k$, entropy, similarity
metrics, LLM judges), so nobody has checked with people what RLVR actually loses; and fixes acting within a
rollout group and across prompts have never been tested together. We address all three gaps on
Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct trained with GRPO on MATH: a pre-registered $2\times3$ factorial crosses a macro factor
(none vs.\ a topic-level budget on positive advantage mass) with a micro factor (none, the per-prompt SELF filter,
or mean-preserving rarity redistribution over solution modes), with two or three seeds per cell, and a blinded
human audit checks what is lost. At our budget of \R{meta.rpp} rollouts per training problem, \RT{R1}{vanilla
GRPO does not shrink the boundary: MATH-500 Pass@1 moves from \R{math.base.p1}\% to \R{math.vanilla.p1}\% and
Pass@32 rises from \R{math.base.p32}\% to \R{math.vanilla.p32}\%, and every condition gains more problems than it
loses. Neither pre-registered contrast is significant. Under the budget, replacing the SELF filter with mode-rarity
redistribution changes the shrinkage slope by \R{math.P1.est}~pp per unit $\ln k$ (95\% CI \R{math.P1.bci}, i.e.\
\R{math.P1.g32} points of gain from $k=1$ to $k=32$), and adding the budget to the redistribution by
\R{math.P2.est} (CI \R{math.P2.bci}).} \RT{R17}{In the blinded audit, two annotators agreed on
\R{human.h1.rawagree}\% of solution pairs (PABAK \R{human.h1.pabak}) and judged \R{human.h1.cons.same} of their
\R{human.h1.consensus} agreed pairs to use the same approach. The word-overlap partitioner that splits them into
``modes'' scores \R{human.h1.acc}\% against that consensus, below a trivial always-same labeller
(\R{human.h1.alwayssame}\%), so the diversity these fixes reweight is mostly wording. The annotators' labels of
reasoning validity agreed no better than chance, leaving what was lost open.} We read the null as a matter of
training intensity rather than model size. The protocol runs on one 24\,GB GPU and is released.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, GRPO, Pass@$k$, reasoning boundary, small language
models, credit assignment, human evaluation, pre-registration
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% =====================================================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================================================
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~\cite{shao2024deepseekmath} and related RLVR methods have become the
standard way to improve mathematical reasoning in open language models. Whether they teach models to solve new
problems, or only to solve solvable ones more reliably, is disputed. Yue et al.~\cite{yue2025rl} found that base
models overtake their RLVR-trained versions when many samples are drawn, a \emph{Pass@$k$ inversion} since analysed
as a shrinking reasoning boundary~\cite{nguyen2025paradox,zhou2026inversion,wu2025leash,zhou2026entrance}. Others
report the opposite: prolonged training expands the boundary~\cite{liu2025prorl}, and RLVR comes out ahead when
only correct chains of thought are counted~\cite{wen2025implicit}; a two-stage account reconciles the two by
training duration~\cite{yao2025debate}. A third view questions the measurement: aggregate declines partly reflect
how few rollouts each training problem receives~\cite{yuan2026overtraining}, and Pass@$k$ at large $k$ rewards
lucky hits~\cite{dragoi2025breadth}. The question matters most for small language models (SLMs), whose usefulness
rests on sampling-based coverage (majority voting, verifier reranking) rather than on one greedy answer.

The evidence on every side is automatic. Pass@$k$ cannot tell a valid solution from a lucky guess; CoT-Pass@$k$
hands that judgment to LLM judges, which accept corrupted reasoning almost as often as clean
reasoning~\cite{tasalti2026cotaudit}; and approach-level diversity has been measured by an LLM judge calibrated on
80 human-labelled pairs, with no human judging RLVR outputs~\cite{lee2026strategy}. To our knowledge, no study has
asked people what RLVR actually loses: whether the solutions that disappear are distinct strategies, and whether
the problems that leave the boundary were ever solved by valid reasoning.

A third gap concerns the fixes. \emph{Intra-group} methods give rare correct modes of one prompt more credit than
common ones~\cite{cao2026cuegrpo,park2026reco,chen2026gcpo,chen2025dragrpo,liu2026edas,cao2026treeadv};
\emph{cross-prompt} methods reweight whole problems or
tasks~\cite{sun2026curverl,yuan2026overtraining,ramesh2026mtgrpo,nguyen2025paradox}. They act on different axes
but have never been combined and tested for complementarity (ReCo combines two corrections, both within one
prompt~\cite{park2026reco}). We address all three gaps in one pre-registered study:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Is shrinkage real at SLM scale?} A multi-seed measurement on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25}
trained on MATH~\cite{hendrycks2021math}, with problem-level boundary entries and exits and the number of rollouts
per training problem~\cite{yuan2026overtraining}.
\item \emph{What is lost, according to people?} A blinded human audit of (H1) whether the solution modes our
partitioner finds are distinct strategies and (H2) whether the base model's successes on problems lost to RLVR
were valid reasoning, against difficulty-matched retained problems.
\item \emph{Do the fixes compose?} A $2\times3$ factorial crossing a topic-level budget on positive advantage mass
(CB, macro) with no micro term, the per-prompt SELF filter, or intra-group mode-rarity redistribution (MEG), with
seed-paired primary contrasts and Holm correction.
\item \RT{R2}{Evidence that at 0.5B and about two rollouts per training problem RLVR expands the boundary slightly
instead of shrinking it, that neither level of fix nor their composite moves the shrinkage slope by more than about
one point per unit $\ln k$, and that correct-solution diversity does not track coverage across runs.}
\end{itemize}
Code, logs, the pre-registration and the annotation protocol are released at \TODO{repository URL}.

% =====================================================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% =====================================================================================================
\textbf{Is shrinkage real?} Yue et al.~\cite{yue2025rl} showed that RLVR-trained models are overtaken by their
base models at large $k$. Nguyen et al.~\cite{nguyen2025paradox} attribute this to negative interference and
winner-take-all reinforcement and propose SELF, which trains only on problems whose greedy answer is wrong; Wu and
Xuan~\cite{wu2025leash} argue that RLVR cannot leave the base model's support, Zhou and Li~\cite{zhou2026entrance}
locate the contraction at the first decision of a solution, and Zhou~\cite{zhou2026inversion} diagnoses the
inversion. Against this, ProRL~\cite{liu2025prorl} reports expansion after prolonged, KL-controlled training, Wen et
al.~\cite{wen2025implicit} report expansion under CoT-Pass@$k$, and Yao et al.~\cite{yao2025debate} reconcile the
two with an exploitation stage that shrinks and an exploration stage that expands. Yuan et
al.~\cite{yuan2026overtraining} relate the decline to few rollouts per problem and gate problems by success count
(BBG), and Dragoi et al.~\cite{dragoi2025breadth} show that Pass@$k$ is biased toward lucky hits. Other responses
change the optimizer or the search~\cite{ba2026es,yu2026datpo,decugis2026fade}. At SLM scale, GRPO
dynamics~\cite{ghosh2026dynamics}, difficulty scaling~\cite{yadav2026difficulty} and reward
granularity~\cite{palandye2026granularity} have been studied, but not shrinkage.

\textbf{Measuring what is lost.} Lee et al.~\cite{lee2026strategy} show that embedding similarity tracks phrasing
more than strategy, that word-bigram overlap tracks approach better, and that only 0.7\% of GSM8K problems admit
more than one approach against 33\% on MATH; their RLVR results come from an LLM judge calibrated on 80
human-labelled pairs. Yang et al.~\cite{yang2026strategy} code the strategies of frontier models with AI coders and
human adjudication, without RL. Ta\c{s}alt{\i} et al.~\cite{tasalti2026cotaudit} find that CoT-Pass@$k$ judges accept
corrupted chains, and that Pass@$k$ exceeds CoT-Pass@$k$ by 19.7 points on Qwen2.5-generation solvers. Our audit
puts people directly on RLVR outcomes.

\textbf{Intra-group credit redistribution.} Cue-GRPO~\cite{cao2026cuegrpo} redistributes positive credit over a
partition of the correct rollouts by rarity, leaving incorrect rollouts untouched and restoring the mean; we adopt
its rule as our micro term. ReCo~\cite{park2026reco} reweights against distributional concentration at the response
and token level; GCPO~\cite{chen2026gcpo}, DRA-GRPO~\cite{chen2025dragrpo}, EDAS~\cite{liu2026edas} and
TreeAdv~\cite{cao2026treeadv} reshape advantages using diversity or structure within the group.

\textbf{Cross-prompt reweighting.} MT-GRPO~\cite{ramesh2026mtgrpo} reweights explicit tasks for worst-task
reliability; CurveRL~\cite{sun2026curverl} reweights prompts by their pass-rate distribution; BBG gates problems by
success count~\cite{yuan2026overtraining}; SELF selects by greedy failure~\cite{nguyen2025paradox}. CB differs in
granularity (latent topics rather than tasks or single prompts), in signal (each topic's share of
positive advantage mass), and in mechanism (a stateful multiplicative gate). Our question is not which gate is
best but whether a topic-level and an intra-group intervention compose.

% =====================================================================================================
\section{Method}
% =====================================================================================================
\subsection{GRPO with gated advantages}
For a prompt $x$ the policy $\pi_\theta$ samples a group of $G$ completions $y_1,\dots,y_G$ with binary rewards
$r_i\in\{0,1\}$ (answer correctness). GRPO~\cite{shao2024deepseekmath} uses the group-normalized advantage
\begin{equation}
\Ahat_i = \frac{r_i-\operatorname{mean}(r)}{\operatorname{std}(r)+\epsilon}.
\label{eq:adv}
\end{equation}
Every condition in this study multiplies it by a non-negative gate weight, $\Atil_i = g_i\,\Ahat_i$ with
$g_i = g^{\mathrm{mac}}_i\, g^{\mathrm{mic}}_i$, and minimizes the PPO-clip loss~\cite{schulman2017ppo},
averaged over all $T$ completion tokens in the batch~\cite{yu2025dapo}:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|}
\min\!\big(\rho_{i,t}\Atil_i,\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)\,\Atil_i\big),
\label{eq:loss}
\end{equation}
where $\rho_{i,t}$ is the token probability ratio. Updates are on-policy and use no KL penalty. Vanilla GRPO is
$g_i\equiv1$. Fig.~\ref{fig:method} summarizes the pipeline.

\centering

\subsection{Macro gate: topic budget (CB)}
Topics are the $C=7$ MATH subjects. After each step, CB updates an exponential moving average of each topic's
\emph{spend}, the mean positive advantage mass of its rollouts in that step,
$s_c \leftarrow (1-\eta)\,s_c + \eta\,\operatorname{mean}_{i:c(x_i)=c}\max(\Ahat_i,0)$, with
$\eta=\cbEta$. Spend counts only positive mass, so corrective negative gradient never uses up a topic's budget.
With the overspend ratio $\rho_c = s_c / \tfrac{1}{C}\sum_{c'} s_{c'}$, the gate is
\begin{equation}
\tilde g_c = \delta^{\max(0,\ \rho_c-\vartheta)},\qquad \vartheta=\cbTheta,\ \delta=\cbDelta ,
\label{eq:cb}
\end{equation}
so a topic at $1.5\times$ the average spend gets half the credit of an in-budget one ($\delta^{0.4}=0.5$).
The gate acts only on rollouts with positive advantage. Their weights $\tilde g_{c(x_i)}$ are clipped to
$[0.3,3]$ and rescaled to mean 1 over the step, so CB moves positive credit from over-spending topics to the
others rather than lowering the effective learning rate; negative advantages are left alone. The original
specification ($\vartheta=1.5$, $\delta=0.98$, down-weighting only) never fired in the pilot (spend ratios stayed
within $[0.38,1.46]$), so we changed it before any main run; the pre-registration records this.

\subsection{Micro gates: SELF filter and mode-rarity redistribution (MEG)}
\textbf{SELF.} Following~\cite{nguyen2025paradox}, a prompt whose greedy answer is already correct gets
$g^{\mathrm{self}}_x=\lambda$ ($\lambda=0$, a hard filter), otherwise 1. The greedy answer is decoded as one extra
row of the same generation call (its logits are pinned to the argmax), so it costs one sequence per prompt. We
implement the selection rule only, not SELF's forward-KL term.

\textbf{MEG.} Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the $N$ correct rollouts of a group, partitioned into solution modes, and let
$|M(i)|$ be the size of the mode containing rollout $i$. Following Cue-GRPO~\cite{cao2026cuegrpo},
\begin{equation}
w_i = \frac{N\,|M(i)|^{-\alpha}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}|M(j)|^{-\alpha}}\quad (i\in\mathcal{C}),\qquad
w_i = 1\quad (i\notin\mathcal{C}),
\label{eq:meg}
\end{equation}
with $\alpha=\megAlpha$; weights are clipped to $[0.3,3]$ and rescaled to mean~1 over $\mathcal{C}$. Because the
mean is preserved, MEG changes \emph{which} correct solutions receive credit, not how much; an earlier
down-weight-only version was confounded with a lower learning rate. We call this term the mode-equalizing gate.

\textbf{Mode partitioner.} Modes come from agglomerative clustering of the correct completions, either on
MiniLM~\cite{wang2020minilm} sentence embeddings~\cite{reimers2019sbert} (cosine threshold) or on word-bigram
Jaccard distance. Because embeddings track phrasing more than strategy~\cite{lee2026strategy}, the partitioner is
not hand-tuned: a pre-registered rule, applied to base-model rollouts before training, picks the candidate whose
median number of modes per group lies in $[2,4]$ and is closest to 3 (ties go to bigram). It selected
\R{meta.partitioner} (median \R{meta.calib.modes} modes; \R{meta.calib.multishare}\% of groups with more than one
mode; Table~\ref{tab:calib}). The rejected embedding candidates illustrate the risk: at the thresholds commonly used,
\RT{R15}{they place almost every group's correct rollouts in a single mode}, which would turn MEG into a no-op.

% =====================================================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
% =====================================================================================================
\textbf{Training.} We train Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} with LoRA~\cite{hu2021lora} adapters on the
MATH training split~\cite{hendrycks2021math} (7{,}496 problems with a boxed answer), prompted with the standard
``reason step by step and put the final answer in \texttt{\textbackslash boxed\{\}}'' instruction;
Table~\ref{tab:hparams} lists every setting. Rewards are binary correctness checked with
Math-Verify~\cite{mathverify} under a time limit, with a guarded symbolic fallback; a strict tag-format reward
was dropped after it proved identically zero, hence inert under group normalization. The budget amounts to
\R{meta.epochs} epochs, or \R{meta.rpp} rollouts per training problem. Seed $s$ fixes the data order and LoRA
initialization across conditions, so conditions are compared in seed-paired blocks.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Training and evaluation settings, identical for all conditions.}
\label{tab:hparams}
\centering\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{0.68\columnwidth}@{}}
\toprule

Adapters & LoRA $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout 0, all projections \\
Optimizer & AdamW, lr \R{meta.lr}, cosine, 10\% warm-up, grad-norm clip 1.0 \\
Batch & 16 prompts $\times$ $G{=}8$ rollouts $=128$ rollouts per step \\
Steps & \R{meta.steps}; MATH levels \R{meta.levels} \\
Sampling & $T{=}0.7$, top-$p$ 0.95, no top-$k$, $\le$1{,}024 new tokens \\
Loss & PPO-clip $\varepsilon{=}0.2$, on-policy, token-level mean, no KL \\
CB / SELF / MEG & $\eta{=}\cbEta$, $\vartheta{=}\cbTheta$, $\delta{=}\cbDelta$ / $\lambda{=}0$ / $\alpha{=}\megAlpha$, clip $[0.3,3]$ \\

Hardware & NVIDIA A10G 24\,GB (AWS g5.xlarge), one run per GPU, two GPUs in parallel \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Evaluation.} Every model, including the base model, is scored on the same problems: all of
MATH-500~\cite{lightman2023verify} (1{,}024 tokens), with $n=32$ samples per problem at temperature 0.6 and
top-$p$ 0.95. Pass@$k$ for $k\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\}$ uses the unbiased
estimator~\cite{chen2021codex} $1-\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$ for $c$ correct samples. MATH-500 shares no problem
statement with the training split; 7 of its problems (1.4\%) are template siblings of training problems with a
different question or numbers.

\textbf{Outcome.} The pre-registered primary outcome is the \emph{shrinkage slope}: the least-squares slope of
$\Delta(k)=\text{Pass@}k(\text{run})-\text{Pass@}k(\text{base})$ against $\ln k$, reported in percentage points per
unit $\ln k$. A negative slope means gains at small $k$ turn into losses at large $k$; higher means less shrinkage.
We also count \emph{boundary exits} (problems the base model solves at least once in 32 samples and the trained
model never does) and \emph{entries} (the reverse).

\textbf{Pre-registered analysis.} All contrasts are linear combinations of condition slopes, paired by seed. The
two primary contrasts are P1, \cond{CB$\times$MEG} $-$ \cond{CB$\times$SELF} (intra-group redistribution vs.\
per-prompt filtering, both under the budget), and P2, \cond{CB$\times$MEG} $-$ \cond{MEG} (does the macro level
add to the micro level?). Secondary contrasts are the two macro$\times$micro interactions (S1 for MEG, S2 for
SELF), reported as 95\% bounds rather than verdicts, and the macro main effect (S3); E1 is exploratory.
Each contrast gets a $t$-interval over seeds and a hierarchical bootstrap that resamples seeds and problems
jointly (2{,}000 resamples). An effect is claimed only if its Holm-adjusted~\cite{holm1979simple} bootstrap
$p<0.05$ \emph{and} its bootstrap interval excludes zero. Diagnostics, logged for every condition: normalized
mode entropy of the correct rollouts in each group, the mean gate weight on positive-advantage rollouts, and the
share of prompts SELF selects. The pre-registration also fixes how outcomes are worded: a significant P1 or P2
means the composition helps beyond its parts; if neither is significant and the intervals are narrow, the result
is a bounded null; if vanilla GRPO shows no shrinkage, that is itself reported and the contrasts are still given.

\textbf{Human audit (pre-registered, secondary).} Two annotators \TODO{background}, blind to condition,
group and partitioner output, label two sheets built by our release. \emph{H1, partition validity:}
\R{human.h1.items} pairs of correct base-model solutions to the same training problem, half placed in one mode by
the partitioner and half in different modes, labelled \textsc{same} or \textsc{different} approach under the
approach-level definition of~\cite{lee2026strategy}. We report Cohen's $\kappa$ and the partitioner's balanced
accuracy against the annotators' consensus, and read the modes as approach-level only if it reaches 70\%.
\emph{H2, what is lost:} MATH-500 problems the base model solves at least once in 32 samples but vanilla GRPO never
solves in a majority of seeds (\emph{exited}), each matched to a retained problem with the closest base solve
count. For one random correct base-model solution per problem, annotators judge the reasoning \textsc{valid} or
\textsc{flawed} (right answer, unsupported reasoning). Rates are compared with a two-sided Fisher exact test; the
pre-registered reading is ``mostly lucky hits'' if the exited rate is below 50\% and significantly below the
retained rate, ``genuine loss'' if it is at least 50\% and not significantly lower, ``mixed'' otherwise.

\textbf{Reproducibility.} The pre-registration (committed \TODO{date + commit hash} before any main run), configs,
logs, correctness matrices and the script that generates every number here are released at \TODO{repository URL}.

\subsection{Shrinkage at 0.5B}
\RT{R3}{Vanilla GRPO does not reproduce the inversion at this budget.} Pass@1 moves from \R{math.base.p1}\% to
\R{math.vanilla.p1}\% and Pass@32 rises from \R{math.base.p32}\% to \R{math.vanilla.p32}\% (Table~\ref{tab:main});
the curve stays above zero up to $k=32$ and its slope is positive (\R{math.vanilla.slope}; Fig.~\ref{fig:curves},
left). On average \R{math.vanilla.entered} problems enter the boundary and \R{math.vanilla.exited} leave it. Every
other condition shows the same pattern, a positive slope and more entries than exits. Each training problem received
\R{meta.rpp} rollouts on average, and aggregate shrinkage has been tied to how often each problem is
revisited~\cite{yuan2026overtraining}; our runs sit at the low-visit end that SLM budgets allow.

\subsection{What each level does}
Mode entropy of the correct rollouts starts at \R{meta.entropy0} and \RT{R7}{does not decay under vanilla GRPO}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:curves}, right). Its training mean is \R{math.vanilla.entropy} for \cond{Vanilla} and
\R{math.heg.entropy} for \cond{CB$\times$MEG}. At evaluation, vanilla's correct answers to a problem fall into
\R{mech.vanilla.modes} solution modes on average, against \R{mech.base.modes} for the base model, and its largest mode
holds \R{mech.vanilla.top}\% of them against \R{mech.base.top}\%. There is no collapse for MEG to undo. \cond{SELF}
skips the \R{meta.selrate}\% of prompts it already solves, keeping a mean positive weight of \R{math.self.posw}.
Changes are uneven across subjects (Fig.~\ref{fig:subjects}): under vanilla GRPO, Pass@32 rises by
\R{subj.cp.vanilla}~pp in Counting \& Probability but \R{subj.geo.vanilla}~pp in Geometry. \RT{R8}{The macro gate
binds but changes nothing: in the CB runs a subject's share of positive credit does not predict its Pass@32 change
(Spearman $\rho=\R{mech.topic.rho}$, $n=\R{mech.topic.n}$ subject-runs), so the premise of a topic budget finds no
support here.}

\subsection{What is lost: the human audit}
\textbf{H1, are the modes approaches?} \RT{R17}{The annotators called \R{human.h1.A.same} and \R{human.h1.B.same}
of the \R{human.h1.items} pairs the same approach, although the partitioner had split half of them into different
modes. They agreed on \R{human.h1.consensus} pairs (\R{human.h1.rawagree}\%): \R{human.h1.cons.same}
\textsc{same} and \R{human.h1.cons.diff} \textsc{different}. Cohen's $\kappa$ is only \R{human.h1.kappa} because
almost all labels fall in one class, which depresses $\kappa$ however well raters agree; the prevalence-adjusted
PABAK is \R{human.h1.pabak}. Against the consensus the partitioner scores \R{human.h1.acc}\%, below the
\R{human.h1.alwayssame}\% of a labeller that always answers \textsc{same}: it splits pairs that people see as one
approach. The pre-registered balanced accuracy, \R{human.h1.bacc}\%, is formally above the 70\% bar, but one of its
classes holds a single pair, so we do not rely on it. We read the modes as surface clusters, and MEG as
redistributing credit over them.}

\textbf{H2, what is lost?} Despite its net gains, vanilla GRPO lost \R{human.h2.exited.total} problems in a
majority of seeds. \RT{R18}{The annotators did not agree on whether the base model's successes on those problems
were valid: A rated \R{human.h2.A.valid} of \R{human.h2.items} solutions valid and B \R{human.h2.B.valid}
($\kappa=\R{human.h2.kappa}$, agreement on \R{human.h2.consensus} items). On those items, \R{human.h2.exited.rate}\%
of exited solutions were valid (CI \R{human.h2.exited.ci}, $n=\R{human.h2.exited.n}$) against
\R{human.h2.retained.rate}\% of retained ones (CI \R{human.h2.retained.ci}, $n=\R{human.h2.retained.n}$; Fisher
$p=\R{human.h2.p}$). Read literally, the pre-registered rule gives a genuine loss, but a small subset selected by
agreement at chance-level reliability cannot carry that. Each annotator alone also rated exited solutions valid
more often (A: \R{human.h2.A.exited} vs.\ \R{human.h2.A.retained}, $p=\R{human.h2.A.p}$; B: \R{human.h2.B.exited} vs.\
\R{human.h2.B.retained}, $p=\R{human.h2.B.p}$), without significance.} The audit gives no support for the lucky-hit
reading and does not establish the opposite; we report H2 as inconclusive.

% =====================================================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}
% =====================================================================================================
\RT{R13}{\textbf{Training intensity, not size.} With about two rollouts per training problem and a policy that
moved little (final KL to the base model about an order of magnitude above its bf16 noise floor), RLVR on a 0.5B
model expands the boundary slightly. This is what accounts that tie shrinkage to repeated reinforcement of
saturated problems~\cite{yuan2026overtraining} or to a long exploitation phase~\cite{yao2025debate} predict, and the
inversions reported elsewhere~\cite{yue2025rl,nguyen2025paradox} come from far longer training. We therefore read
our null as evidence about the training regime a single-GPU budget reaches, not about model size, and it suggests a
direct test: raise rollouts per problem at 0.5B and shrinkage should appear. Fixes designed against shrinkage have
little to act on in this regime.} \textbf{The partition is the weak link.} Embedding partitions put nearly every
group into one mode (Table~\ref{tab:calib}); the bigram partition we selected finds about three modes that people see
as one approach. Neither tracks what intra-group methods assume it tracks, which matters for any method that
reweights over such partitions~\cite{cao2026cuegrpo,park2026reco,chen2026gcpo,chen2025dragrpo,liu2026edas}. This is
compatible with Lee et al.'s finding that a third of MATH problems admit more than one approach~\cite{lee2026strategy}:
the alternatives exist in the dataset but rarely in what a 0.5B model samples. We do not claim that shrinkage is
absent at larger budgets; the bounds in Table~\ref{tab:contrasts} are what a longer study would need to beat.

\textbf{Limitations.} One model at one size; LoRA, one RL algorithm and short training (\R{meta.steps} steps, cut
from a planned 240), evaluated only on MATH-500. Two or three seeds per cell leave the interactions open. SELF
omits its forward-KL term, and no random-partition control was run. The audit has two non-author annotators who
differed in strictness on H2, and the pre-registered third annotator was not used. The correlations in
Section~V-C are descriptive and were added after the pre-registration.

% =====================================================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================================================
In a pre-registered study of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with a blinded human audit, \RT{R14}{shrinkage does not appear
at about two rollouts per training problem, and neither a topic-level budget, intra-group mode-rarity
redistribution, nor their composite moves the shrinkage slope by more than about one point per unit $\ln k$}.
People judged the partitioner's modes to be wording variants of one approach. The protocol runs on a single
24\,GB GPU in \R{meta.gpuh} GPU-hours and is released.
